newsitem.title: UK: United names price for BA/American deal.
newsitem.headline: United names price for BA/American deal.

text.p: United Airlines said on Tuesday it wants British Airways and American Airlines to give up 30 takeoff and landing slots at London's Heathrow airport as the main price for ending its opposition to their proposed alliance.

United's government affairs team told reporters that its proposals would also satisfy United's demands for concessions from the British government in the related Anglo-U.S. aviation trade talks which resume in London on Wednesday.

United said it would be satisfied if BA and American agreed to make room on the congested runways at Heathrow, Chicago and New York's JFK airport to allow new competition in to counterbalance the BA/American combination on six transatlantic routes where BA and American would otherwise be dominant.
This would involve transferring 30 daily slots at London Heathrow, six at Chicago and 12 at JFK to allow rivals to introduce new competition.

Otherwise United said the BA/American combination would start with a monopoly on Boston-Heathrow and Miami-Heathrow as well as Dallas to London Gatwick, and a dominant 87 percent share of the Chicago-Heathrow market, 66 percent share of JFK-Heathrow and 53 percent of Los Angles-Heathrow.
"We think this is a very precise formula to solve this problem," said Cyril Murphy, United's vice-president for international affairs.
"This will allow the US Department of Transportation to reallocate slots to carriers willing to provide competing services in those markets."
Murphy said United now had to present the plan to U.S. government aviation negotiators and the competition authorities.

Under the proposals, Murphy said, BA and American would be allowed to redeploy their other runway slots to maintain their frequencies on these routes or to try and acquire more slots through the industry's normal trading mechanisms.

Under the proposed alliance BA intends to coordinate its 244 flights a week from Britain to 22 U.S. destinations with all of American's 238 flights a week from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.

BA and American have argued that their deal will lead to greater competition because it will only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. agree "open skies" allowing all U.S. airlines access to Heathrow, the world's busiest international airport and the most popular of all of Europe's transatlantic landfalls.

Under the current aviation agreement dating back to March 1991 only British Airways, Virgin Atlantic Airways, American and United are allowed to use Heathrow for transatlantic services, and their frequencies and routes are restricted.

But open skies talks broke down again in August amidst complaints by rival U.S. carriers that Heathrow is so crowded that open access would be meaningless unless they were to be granted some of British Airways' share of slots, which currently amounts to 38 percent and would increase to 42 percent under the alliance with American.

BA refuses to give up slots, saying other carriers have a bigger share of slots at their home hubs and airlines should find their own slots by waiting their turn in the normal processes of trading and allocation at Heathrow.

"We see no justification for relinquishing takeoff and landing slots," a company spokesman said on Tuesday. "There has been no statement from the government to suggest that that will be a requirement and it is obviously premature to make any such suggestion. Other major airline alliances have not been required to give up any slots or make any concessions to have their transtatlantic alliances approved," he said.
